column6: The commentary makes patience the act of holding one's own self; the proverb ranks the person who rules his spirit above a conqueror, turning restraint into strength.

The commentary contrasts self-restraint with being held by another; this proverb pictures a person without control of spirit as a city without walls, exposed precisely because the inner guard is absent.
The commentary defines patience as keeping the self from outcry; the psalmist says he has calmed and quieted his soul like a weaned child, giving that inner action a concrete image.
The commentary's patient person holds the self back from lament; the psalmist resolves to muzzle his mouth while the wicked stand before him, an intentional restraint of speech.
The commentary places the holding hand alongside restraint of the person; Job recalls princes stopping their words and putting a hand over their mouth, a visible enactment of self-control.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's asr includes restraining; Eliphaz asks who can restrain words when provoked, using Hebrew עצר for the failure of verbal self-control.

The commentary's passive captive is held for killing, while its patient person withholds an outcry; the servant is led like a lamb to slaughter and does not open his mouth, joining both positions in one scene.
The commentary contrasts being held by others with holding oneself; Jesus, under abuse, neither retaliates nor threatens but entrusts judgment to God, giving the captive person's restraint agency.

column5: captivity and the endurance of saints
column6: The commentary opposes the person held by others to the one who practices patience; this verse names captivity and sword death, then identifies the saints' endurance and faith in that situation.
The commentary's prisoner is held toward death and the believer is urged to endure; the church is warned of imprisonment and called to remain faithful even to death.

The commentary calls fasting one form of holding the self and also depicts a person held against his will; Isaiah calls for a fast that loosens bonds and frees the oppressed, joining the two types of holding ethically.
The commentary juxtaposes fasting as restraint and the hand that withholds what it could give; Isaiah's chosen fast requires sharing bread with the hungry and bringing the homeless in.

column5: closing the hand to the poor
column6: The commentary's tight-handed asir keeps back what he can give; the law forbids hardening the heart or closing the hand against a poor brother.
The commentary depicts the person who holds his hand against giving; this verse commands opening the hand and lending enough for the poor person's need.
The commentary calls the withholding hand a form of asr; the proverb forbids keeping good from those to whom it is due when one's hand has power to do it.
The commentary links the tight hand to the human being in loss; this proverb says one person withholds what ought to be given and comes to want, giving that loss an economic form.
The commentary's asir has the means to give but holds them; the letter asks how God's love remains in a person who sees a needy brother yet closes compassion while possessing worldly goods.

column5: failure to feed and give drink
column6: The commentary treats the withholding hand as a moral failure; the condemned are told they gave no food or drink to the hungry and thirsty, making a withheld gift decisive in judgment.

column5: wealth holder begs relief from flame
column6: The commentary places withholding beside daring toward fire; the rich man who ignored Lazarus now begs for a finger dipped in water to cool him in the flame, reversing who needs the other's hand.
The commentary's gain-hoarding person becomes the one held to loss; Abraham tells the rich man that Lazarus now receives comfort while he is in anguish, explaining the reversal after their lifetimes.

The commentary pairs a bad purchase with loss and fire; Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life, a pointed counterpart to buying error at the cost of guidance.

The commentary's inverted patience is brazen acceptance of fire after a bad bargain; Daniel's companions refuse the idol even without rescue, making courage before threatened fire serve fidelity instead.
The commentary's wrongdoers are daring toward punitive fire; in Daniel the king sees the faithful captives walking unharmed in the furnace, reversing the moral reason for facing fire and its outcome.
The commentary includes the hand that withholds available goods; Lazarus longs for the crumbs from the rich man's table, so the later flame follows a specific unshared surplus.

The commentary's phrase about daring toward fire exposes the folly of accepting destructive consequences; the proverb asks whether one can carry fire against the chest without burning one's clothes, in its context a warning against adultery.

The commentary links a ruinous choice to apparent boldness before fire; those who kindle their own fire are told to walk by its flames and will lie down in torment, making the chosen flame a judgment.
The commentary places a withholding hand beside fire as a dire end; the judgment scene sends those on the left to eternal fire, with their failure to feed and welcome specified in the next verse.

column5: king imposes oath and food restraint
column6: The commentary distinguishes chosen fasting from a man forcibly made to swear; Saul binds his troops with an oath not to eat until evening, turning restraint into an imposed burden.

column5: fear of oath keeps hands from food
column6: The commentary depicts forced oath and a restrained hand; Saul's troops see honey but no one puts a hand to his mouth because they fear the oath, showing bodily cost of imposed restraint.
The commentary's captive is made to swear and faces death; the high priest adjures the previously silent Jesus by the living God to answer about his identity during the trial.
The commentary names a father holding back his son's property; the angel says Abraham has not withheld his son from God, reversing the direction and object of a father's withholding.

column5: limit on father's disposal of inheritance
column6: The commentary pictures a father holding back what belongs to a son; the law bars a father from favoring a later son with the firstborn's portion, constraining paternal control of property.

column5: father divides property at son's request
column6: The commentary's father withholds a child's goods; the younger son requests his share and the father divides the estate, a narrative reversal of paternal withholding.

column5: father says all his goods are son's
column6: The commentary raises the possibility of a father retaining a son's property; the father assures the elder son that everything he has is his, distinguishing possession from a closed paternal hand.
The commentary's newly menstruating girl is kept at home; this law situates a young woman's vow while she remains in her father's house, where his authority can affect her commitment.
The commentary's held girl is subject to a household's control; the father can forbid the vow he hears and the daughter is released from it, a concrete form of paternal restraint in that house.

column5: father's authority over minor daughter's goods and vows
column6: The commentary joins a father controlling a child's property with a young girl kept at home; this legal tradition enumerates a father's rights over his minor daughter's betrothal, earnings, finds and vows, clarifying how household custody includes economic control.

column5: Mary removed from temple at puberty
column6: The commentary calls the newly menstruating girl one kept in the house; the priests seek a guardian for twelve-year-old Mary lest her approaching maturity defile the sanctuary, an early Christian account of seclusion and relocation around puberty.
The commentary extends self-restraint from a person to a community; Joel orders a sanctified fast and calls a solemn assembly, using the table's Hebrew עצר family for the collective gathering.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's asr includes holding back; the seventh day is an עצרת, a restrained festival assembly in which no work is done, joining communal gathering to a prohibition on action.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's passive patient is confined by others; the Assyrian king confines Hoshea and binds him in prison, using Hebrew עצר for involuntary custody.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary pairs being held with a divine word received while waiting; Jeremiah is still confined in the court of the guard when the Lord's word comes to him, using עצר for custody.

column5: Lord's eye on those who wait
column6: The commentary tells the waiting prophet that he is under God's eyes; this psalm says the Lord's eye rests on those who fear him and wait for his faithful love, joining watchfulness to expectation.
The commentary's patient servant waits under divine sight; the seer says the Lord's eyes range through the earth to strengthen those fully loyal to him, making observation a source of support.

column5: God's eyes and ears attend the righteous
column6: The commentary says the waiting person is under God's eyes; this letter applies the scriptural formula of the Lord's eyes toward the righteous and ears toward their prayer, giving the watched person a hearing as well.
The commentary invokes the fish's owner as the example a patient prophet must avoid; the Hebrew story first has a great fish swallow Jonah, making his literal confinement the setting of that warning.
The commentary recalls the fish's owner crying out while constrained; in Hebrew verse numbering Jonah prays to the Lord from the fish's belly, turning confinement into an appeal.
The commentary warns the waiting prophet not to be like the constricted fish's owner; later Jonah tells God he is angry enough to die, identifying the uncontrolled reaction at issue.
The commentary defines patience as waiting under God's judgment without outcry; Lamentations calls it good to wait quietly for the Lord's salvation amid suffering.

column5: sitting alone in silence under imposed burden
column6: The commentary distinguishes holding oneself from being held by another; the sufferer is told to sit alone and silent because a yoke has been laid on him, holding both experiences together.
The commentary's patience includes waiting rather than merely suppression; James asks believers to be patient until the Lord's coming like a farmer awaiting the crop and its rains.
The commentary tells the prophet to wait for the Lord's judgment; Hebrews says believers need endurance to do God's will and receive what was promised, connecting delay with obedient action.

column5: God limits trial and makes endurance possible
column6: The commentary joins patient endurance to being under divine care; Paul says God will not allow a trial beyond capacity and will provide a way to endure it.
The commentary makes patience something believers commend to each other; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation lest any heart be hardened by sin.

column5: spur one another to love and good works
column6: The commentary's mutual counsel sits beside faith and righteous action; Hebrews asks members to consider how to provoke one another toward love and good deeds.

column5: mutual encouragement as the day approaches
column6: The commentary expands restraint to a persevering group; Hebrews warns against abandoning assembly and calls for encouraging one another as the day draws near.

column5: warn, encourage, support, be patient with all
column6: The commentary's patience is a shared duty rather than an isolated virtue; Paul orders the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient toward all.

column5: bear with and forgive one another
column6: The commentary calls believers to recommend patience to one another; Colossians makes that reciprocal by asking each person to bear with and forgive another after a complaint.
The commentary extends the held self to a community that holds together; Ephesians names patience and bearing with one another in love as conduct worthy of the calling.
The commentary groups faith, good action and mutual patience as the exception to loss; Revelation identifies the saints' endurance with keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus.
The commentary puts faith beside patience in the saved community; Hebrews tells readers to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience.

column5: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
column6: The commentary's insan is vulnerable to loss yet addressed by divine care; the psalm asks why God remembers mortal enosh, setting human frailty beside God's attention.

column5: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
column6: The commentary's insan is one held under divine judgment; Job asks why God makes so much of mortal enosh and sets his heart on him, casting close attention as oppressive in his suffering.
The commentary says the patient waits under God's eyes as protection; Job complains that God visits and tests him every morning, preserving a contrary experience of divine surveillance.

column5: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's insan is mortal and at risk of loss; Daniel sees a figure like a son of enash coming with the clouds toward the Ancient of Days, giving the human designation a strikingly exalted setting.

column5: kingdom granted to the humanlike figure
column6: The commentary describes humanity in loss and then an exception; the figure introduced as a son of enash in the previous verse receives an enduring dominion here, making the reversal explicit.

column5: kingdom given to oppressed holy people
column6: The commentary makes believing endurance the exception to human loss; after the preceding vision of oppression, Daniel gives the kingdom to the people of the holy ones, a corporate reversal of defeat.

column5: fear of dying mortal against divine comfort
column6: The commentary calls the human being frail and liable to loss; God asks why the comforted people fear mortal enosh who dies like grass, while divine reassurance remains available.

column5: mortal man heaps wealth without knowing heir
column6: The commentary's tight hand is set beside humanity's loss; this psalm says a person heaps wealth without knowing who will gather it, using צבר, the table's sound match to ص ب ر, here meaning accumulation rather than patience.

column5: wait for God after futile hoarding
column6: The commentary opposes possessive holding to patient waiting; immediately after describing a person heaping goods without knowing their heir, the psalmist asks what he waits for and names God as hope.

The commentary's withholding hand accumulates goods under threat of loss; Job says the wicked may heap up silver like dust, using צבר, the table's sound match to ص ب ر with the distinct sense of accumulation.

column5: stored goods pass to the innocent
column6: The commentary's human holder cannot keep his gain secure; Job says the innocent will divide the wicked person's silver, reversing the hoard described in the preceding verse.

column5: Tyre heaps wealth behind a fortress
column6: The commentary associates protected stores with a potentially grasping hand; Tyre builds a stronghold and heaps silver and gold like dust, using צבר, the table's sound match to ص ب ر with the distinct sense of piling up.

column5: stored wealth lost and city consumed by fire
column6: The commentary links hoarding with ultimate fire; after Tyre's fortified accumulation, the Lord strips its wealth and fire consumes it, showing how a guarded store fails.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's asr can enclose a girl at reproductive maturity; Sarai says the Lord has restrained her from bearing children, using עצר for an involuntary bodily restriction rather than household confinement.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's house-held girl connects enclosure with reproduction; God has closed the wombs throughout Abimelech's household because of Sarah, using עצר for reproductive restraint, a different subject and cause.

column5: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's collective patience joins moral action to communal holding; God rejects an עצרה, a solemn assembly, when worship is mixed with injustice, warning that the gathered form alone does not suffice.
The commentary allows holding to describe a whole community; the eighth-day sacred assembly, called עצרת from the table's Hebrew עצר family, is paired with a ban on ordinary work.

column5: grain is crushed but not endlessly
column6: The commentary's grain is protected in its covering; Isaiah distinguishes grain processing from destruction, saying it is threshed but not pulverized forever, an agricultural counterpart to protection before use.
The commentary imagines grain sheltered in its covering; the winnower separates wheat from chaff and gathers the grain into storage, showing the covering removed when preservation takes a new form.
The commentary's enclosed grain is kept for safety; Joseph proposes keeping grain as a reserve for famine so the land will not perish, shifting protection from a husk to a storehouse.
The commentary's grain is something held in reserve; Joseph stores so much grain that it becomes uncountable, a beneficial form of withholding set against the commentary's selfish tight hand.

The commentary's grain remains protected in its covering; Jesus says a grain that does not fall into the earth and die remains alone, while dying makes it fruitful, a contrary claim about when protected seed must be released.

The commentary makes fasting a kind of self-restraint yet warns about holding others; Isaiah rebukes fasters who pursue their own business and oppress workers on the fast day, exposing the split between the two acts.

column5: communal fast judged by changed deeds
column6: The commentary broadens patience to a community and calls fasting a form of restraint; this fast-day exhortation says the people of Nineveh were heeded for changed deeds, making a gathered fast accountable to conduct.
The commentary treats fasting as an inward holding of the self; Jesus warns fasters against disfiguring their faces to be seen by others, distinguishing the act from theatrical self-display.

The commentary connects patience with waiting and fasting with self-restraint; Jesus says the wedding guests will fast when the bridegroom is taken away, giving voluntary abstinence the time of an absence.
The commentary extends patient holding from a person to a group; the Antioch church worships and fasts when the Spirit speaks, placing shared restraint beside guidance and action.
The commentary makes fasting one form of patience in a community; the Didache prescribes shared weekly fast days, showing how the act became a repeated group discipline.
The commentary defines patience as holding the self rather than being held; the saying calls one who conquers his own inclination mighty, interpreting power as inward mastery.

The commentary's holding hand can be stingy; the Didache asks that alms remain in the hand until the giver knows the recipient, a distinct form of temporary restraint meant to guide giving rather than avoid it.

The commentary's asir withholds resources; this church exhortation tells the rich to supply the poor person's need and the poor to thank God for the provider, turning possession into a reciprocal relation.
The commentary sets forced oath beside the tight hand; Paul tells each person to give as decided in the heart, not under compulsion, so the release of goods is neither hoarding nor coercion.

column5: good wishes without food or clothing
column6: The commentary makes withheld goods a failure of the hand; James asks what good it does to wish warmth and fullness to a needy person without providing bodily necessities.
The commentary's asir is marked by a hand held closed; the righteous person in this proverb gives and does not hold back, after the preceding clause describes craving all day.
The commentary names a father withholding a son's goods; the proverb praises a good person who leaves an inheritance to grandchildren, a long view of wealth passed on rather than retained.

column5: father asked for bread does not give stone
column6: The commentary imagines a father's hand controlling what his child receives; Jesus' question assumes a father responds to a son's request for bread with food rather than a useless stone.
The commentary includes grain kept in protection and wealth held back; the rich farmer plans larger barns for his grain and goods, joining storage to the closed-hand danger.
The commentary's possessor is still a mortal held to account; God demands the rich farmer's life that night and asks who will own the stored goods, overturning the fantasy of secure possession.

column5: ء ن س / אנס, table sound match; compulsion, not human cognate
column6: The commentary's forced oath shows one person restraining another; Esther's banquet rule says drinking is without compulsion, a specific reversal of social coercion, though the act is drinking rather than swearing and the Hebrew root is not used for a human being.
The commentary mentions a man made to swear by another; Solomon's prayer envisages an oath being laid on an accused man at the altar and asks God to judge, giving imposed swearing a judicial setting.

column5: truthful speech in place of oaths
column6: The commentary's oath scene makes another person control a man's speech; James forbids oath-taking and asks for plain yes and no, a response to the moral vulnerability of sworn speech.

column5: confined speaker sends his words outward
column6: The commentary contrasts a held person with mutually recommended truth; Jeremiah says he is detained and cannot enter the Lord's house, then instructs Baruch to read his scroll there, showing testimony moving despite confinement.

column5: prisoners pray and sing while bound
column6: The commentary's captive can still practice an active form of patience; Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight in prison while other prisoners listen.

column5: be still while waiting for the Lord
column6: The commentary says waiting is a form of patience under divine judgment; the psalm orders the hearer to be still before the Lord and wait rather than fret over a prospering schemer.
The commentary's prophet is told to endure while awaiting the Lord's decision; James names the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.
The commentary joins waiting under pain to divine care; James calls those who endured blessed and points to Job's endurance and the Lord's compassionate outcome.
The commentary defines patience as holding back lament under misfortune; Job rebukes his wife's counsel and accepts adversity from God without sinning with his lips in this scene.

column5: patient in affliction and constant in prayer
column6: The commentary's waiting person restrains panic under God's eyes; Paul joins patience in suffering to persistence in prayer, making endurance an active appeal.
The commentary moves from one person's held self to shared endurance; Paul commands believers to bear one another's burdens, giving collective patience a practical action.

column5: whole household called out to assembly
column6: The commentary expands holding to a community and evokes domestic enclosure; Joel summons elders, children, nursing infants and even bride and groom from their rooms, showing the fast superseding ordinary household boundaries.

column5: guardian decides about young woman's marriage
column6: The commentary's girl is subject to household control at maturity; one reading of Paul's ambiguous reference to a man's virgin and her passing youth concerns a father's decision about marriage, though the passage can also be read of a betrothed couple.

column5: prisoners groan and are marked for death
column6: The commentary's passive patient is someone held for killing; the psalm asks God to hear imprisoned people's groans and preserve those appointed to die, adding a plea for release to the captive scene.

The commentary's bad exchange is followed by daring toward fire; Ezekiel condemns unjust trading and says fire will come from the trader's midst and consume him, bringing commerce and punishment into one verse.
The commentary says a person can be held as security for what he has earned; the unforgiving servant imprisons a fellow debtor until he pays, making financial liability literal captivity.

column5: unforgiving creditor made the detained debtor
column6: The commentary contrasts the hand that withholds with the one who becomes held; the master hands the unmerciful servant over to jailers until his debt is paid, reversing his role in the previous imprisonment.

The commentary links a father's control of goods to the person forcibly held; indebted families say their daughters are already enslaved and their fields belong to others, showing a household's loss of both property and freedom.

column5: impatient merchants wait out rest to sell grain
column6: The commentary sets patient communal restraint against the grasping hand and protected grain; merchants ask when the new moon and sabbath will end so they can sell grain with dishonest measures, turning waiting into greed.

column5: buying the poor and selling inferior grain
column6: The commentary's bad bargain and tight hand harm other people; Amos accuses merchants of buying the needy for silver and selling sweepings of wheat, joining unjust exchange to grain.
The commentary says humans cry out under harm yet withhold good when they have it; the proverb warns that one who shuts his ear to the poor person's cry will cry out and receive no answer.

column5: unjust gain takes the owner's life
column6: The commentary's bargain for error leads to loss; the proverb says ill-gotten gain takes away the life of its possessors, making acquisition turn against the acquirer.

The commentary's father-and-son property scene raises goods held from rightful users; Nehemiah demands that lenders return debtors' fields and houses and remit the interest, providing a communal remedy for the grasping hand.
The commentary's captive is held toward death; Jesus' reading of Isaiah announces release to captives, supplying a counter movement to the image of enforced confinement.

column5: facing lethal torment for covenant hope
column6: The commentary's inverted patience is rash boldness before fire after rejecting guidance; the tortured brother tells his killer that God will raise those who die for God's laws, a contrary reason for accepting death.

The commentary makes patience a virtue commended between people; the mother watches her seven sons die in one day and bears it with courage because of hope in the Lord, a family form of shared endurance.
